name: Target in the middle
why: The simplest case failed, so the main part of the loop is wrong. Check that you compare platforms[mid] with the target, and that you return mid (the index), not platforms[mid] (the value).

name: Target at index 0
why: To reach the first value, the window must shrink down to index 0. If this fails, the loop probably stops too early, when lo == hi. With a closed window, the loop condition must be `while lo <= hi`.

name: Target at the last index
why: With a closed window, hi must start at len(platforms) - 1. If it starts lower, or the loop stops one pass early, the last value is never checked.

name: Not in the list, smaller than all values
why: Here hi keeps moving left until the window is empty. This test usually fails when the code returns lo or 0 instead of -1, or reads platforms[hi] after the loop when hi is -1.

name: Not in the list, bigger than all values
why: Here lo moves past the end of the list. If you read platforms[lo] after the loop without first checking that lo < len(platforms), you get an IndexError.

name: Not in the list, between two values
why: 12 is between 11 and 14. A common mistake is to return the index where 12 would be inserted (3) instead of -1. After the loop, check that the value really is the target.

name: Empty list
why: With no platforms, hi starts at -1, so the loop must not run at all. An IndexError here means the code reads platforms[0] or platforms[mid] before checking that the window is not empty.

name: One platform, present
why: With one platform, lo == hi. The loop must still run once, so the condition must be `lo <= hi`, not `lo < hi`.

name: One platform, not in the list
why: After one comparison, the window must become empty. If this test runs out of time, one branch sets lo = mid or hi = mid, so the window never gets smaller.

name: Two platforms
why: With two platforms, mid rounds down to the first one. If the branch that moves right uses lo = mid, lo never changes and the test runs out of time. It must be lo = mid + 1.

name: A million platforms, at most 25 reads
why: This list counts every value you read. Binary search needs at most 20 reads for a million values. More than 25 reads means the code goes through the list one value at a time. A for loop, `in`, `.index()`, list(), sorted() and slicing all do this.

name: A million platforms, target not in the list
show: platforms = [0, 2, 4, …, 1999998], target = 1234567 (odd, so not in the list)
why: The same counting list, but the target is missing. This is the worst case for going through the list one by one: it reads all million values. Binary search still needs at most 20 reads.
